power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

Adding emotion category did not significantly improve the model fit relative to the null model (χ²(3) = 0.29, p = 0.96), indicating that the likelihood of reporting mental imagery did not differ across the four intended emotion categories.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. :::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 657 columns across 18 data files.
#### Issues Identified

21 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

ethics_statements: The study was approved by the University of Jyväskylä Ethics Committee, and all methods were carried out in accordance with relevant guidelines and regulations as approved by the JYU IRB.
The study complies with the ethical code and conduct of research under the TENK (2019) guidelines and was approved by the Human Sciences Ethics Committee of the University of Jyväskylä, Finland.
live_data_statements: Participants were recruited through Prolific.
Four participants reported a known hearing impairment.

As hearing ability was not specified as an eligibility criterion during recruitment, and preliminary sensitivity analyses with these participants excluded did not indicate any substantive changes in the results, these participants were retained for subsequent analyses.
All participants provided informed consent prior to participation.
Further, participants were asked to respond to multiple choice questions assessing different characteristics of their imagery experience.
Participants were allowed to select multiple options for each of the above categories.
Beyond this, participants were also asked to provide a free-text description of their imagery experience, allowing for qualitative insights into imagery content.

Regardless of imagery presence, all participants provided subjective music appraisal ratings for each stimulus, including valence (unpleasant-pleasant), arousal (calm-energising), liking and familiarity using continuous slider scales from 0-100.
Following the main experimental task, participants completed a set of questionnaires assessing individual differences relevant to imagery and music processing.
Finally, participants completed a set of demographic questions, including age, gender, hearing status, current country of residence, country of origin and native language.
In addition, participants were asked to report up to two music pieces that they believed effectively elicited mental imagery during listening.
Participants were first presented with an information sheet explaining the study and were asked to confirm their informed consent to participate in the study.
Participants were instructed to conduct the experiment alone in a quiet environment, preferably with headphones to avoid distractions.
Each trial consisted of the presentation of a single 60s music excerpt, during which participants were instructed to listen attentively.
Participants were not allowed to pause, replay or skip the audio clips.
After listening and responding to all 12 music clips, participants completed questions on the individual traits of sensory imagery, musical background and demographics questions.
Finally, the participants were reimbursed for their time after the task was completed.
Open-ended responses provided in language other than English by one participant were translated using DeepL prior to analysis.
Consent to participate Informed consent was obtained from all individual participants included in the study.
Consent for publication Participants were drawn from the crowd-sourcing platform Prolific.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 2 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:2, File = c("MUSIMAGINE__DataCleaning.R", 
"MUSIMAGINE_AnalysisScript.R"), "Runs after" = c("—", "MUSIMAGINE__DataCleaning.R"
), Basis = c("none", "dependency")), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Missing inputs
1 input file the code reads is in the deposit but not usable as named: too large to download, inside an archive, or under a similar name.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "mir_acoustic_features_selected.csv", Status = "absent", 
    Reason = "the deposit holds mir_acoustic_features_selected.xlsx, the code reads mir_acoustic_features_selected.csv"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### Files the deposit does not hold
The scripts that did not run through read 1 data file that is not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: `13428_2013_403_moesm1_esm.xlsx`.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 2 scripts: 0 ran without error, 2 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **1 script stopped on a file another script writes**, so it was run once more after the other scripts: `MUSIMAGINE__DataCleaning.R` (final_data.csv). Which script must run first can be stated in a README, or shown by numbering the file names (01_, 02_).

text.text: Music listening often evokes mental imagery involving imagined scenes, people, movement, emotions, and narratives.

However, systematic research on music-evoked mental imagery (MEMI) requires resources that capture not only whether imagery occurs, but also its phenomenological characteristics, content and potential determinants.
We introduce MUSIMAGINE, an open-access database designed to support multidimensional investigation of MEMI.

The database comprises sixty royalty-free, 60second instrumental excerpts selected to represent four valence-arousal quadrants, alongside data from 153 participants who listened to a subset of the excerpts.

Measures include imagery occurrence; six phenomenological ratings (ease, vividness, clarity, narrativity, movement and emotion intensity); structured reports of imagery elements, sensory modalities, and emotions; open-ended descriptions; subjective music appraisal (valence, arousal, liking, familiarity); individual differences in sensory imagery ability and musical background; and acoustic annotations.
Imagery was reported on approximately 82% of listening trials, although its occurrence varied across excerpts.

Analyses indicated that subjective appraisals of music and individual imagery ability were associated with imagery occurrence, whereas the broad acoustic components examined did not show a significant direct association.
The database also captures variation in the phenomenological characteristics and reported content of imagery experiences through complementary quantitative and qualitative measures.
MUSIMAGINE provides an openly accessible resource for examining relationships among music stimuli, listener characteristics, subjective appraisals, and the occurrence and characteristics of MEMI.
It offers a foundation for further behavioural, computational, and neuroscientific research, while enabling future studies to test and extend patterns observed in the present dataset.
The train pulls away from the platform as the sun begins to set.
A child runs across a field, laughing, while a dog races behind.
The air smells of rain.
You turn onto a quiet street where someone is waiting outside a familiar house.
Their face is just out of view, yet you know exactly who they are.
A sudden gust of wind interrupts the moment, the colours begin to fade, and the scene disappears.
You open your eyes slowly.
Nothing around you has changed.
You have not left your seat, spoken to anyone, or travelled anywhere.
Throughout this entire experience, you have simply been sitting with a pair of headphones on, listening to an unfamiliar piece of instrumental music.
Music listening is seldom restricted to acoustics; it often involves imagined scenes, emotions, narratives, and movements that unfold alongside the auditory experience.

Such experiences are not rare or merely anecdotal, rather, they reflect a widespread phenomenon in which the dynamic and expressive structure of music gives rise to rich forms of mental imagery across sensory and emotional domains (Belfi, 2019; Küssner & Eerola, 2019; Nanay, 2022; Taruffi et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Such experiences are not rare or merely anecdotal, rather, they reflect a widespread phenomenon in which the dynamic and expressive structure of music gives rise to rich forms of mental imagery across sensory and emotional domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Belfi, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Küssner & Eerola, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Nanay, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Taruffi et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: These internally generated experiences, commonly referred to as Music-Evoked Mental Imagery (MEMI) have increasingly attracted attention within music cognition research due to the multisensory, affective and imaginative processes involved in the music perception and interpretation (Küssner et al., 2022).
text.formatted: These internally generated experiences, commonly referred to as Music-Evoked Mental Imagery (MEMI) have increasingly attracted attention within music cognition research due to the multisensory, affective and imaginative processes involved in the music perception and interpretation <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Küssner et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Despite this growing interest, many questions regarding the evaluation, dimensions, and underlying mechanisms of MEMI remain unresolved.
One factor contributing to this lack of clarity is the considerable theoretical and methodological diversity within MEMI research.

Previous research has conceptualised MEMI in substantially different ways, encompassing visual imagery, imagined narratives, emotional and autobiographical experiences, motor imagery or taskirrelevant forms of thought (Herff et al., 2021; Jakubowski et al., 2024; Margulis et al., 2019; Taruffi et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Previous research has conceptualised MEMI in substantially different ways, encompassing visual imagery, imagined narratives, emotional and autobiographical experiences, motor imagery or taskirrelevant forms of thought <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Herff et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Jakubowski et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Margulis et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Taruffi et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Some studies have approached MEMI primarily as a perceptual and phenomenological experience, whereas others have examined it through dimensions like prevalence, vividness, timing, controllability and intensity (Ayyildiz, Milne, et al., 2025; Hashim et al., 2023; Küssner et al., 2022; Margulis, Williams, et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Some studies have approached MEMI primarily as a perceptual and phenomenological experience, whereas others have examined it through dimensions like prevalence, vividness, timing, controllability and intensity <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Ayyildiz, Milne, et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Hashim et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Küssner et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Margulis, Williams, et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, the field encompasses a wide range of methodological approaches including self-reported measures, qualitative descriptions, behavioural paradigms, neurophysiological methods and acoustic analyses (Gelding et al., 2023; Groves et al., 2025; Kosslyn et al., 2001).
text.formatted: Consequently, the field encompasses a wide range of methodological approaches including self-reported measures, qualitative descriptions, behavioural paradigms, neurophysiological methods and acoustic analyses <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Gelding et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Groves et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Kosslyn et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Although these approaches have provided valuable insights into different aspects of MEMI, differences in conceptualisation and measurement can make it difficult to compare findings across studies or establish an integrated framework for evaluating imagery experiences.
The precise definition of mental imagery is notoriously complex, generally referring to a "sensory-like experience in the absence of external stimuli" (Finch & Oakman, 2022).
text.formatted: The precise definition of mental imagery is notoriously complex, generally referring to a "sensory-like experience in the absence of external stimuli" <ref type="bibr">(Finch & Oakman, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In the context of music, however, imagery extends beyond "seeing with the mind's eye" or "hearing with the mind's ear" commonly emphasised in the existing MEMI research (Kosslyn et al., 2001).
text.formatted: In the context of music, however, imagery extends beyond "seeing with the mind's eye" or "hearing with the mind's ear" commonly emphasised in the existing MEMI research <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Kosslyn et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: During music listening, experiences are shaped by prior knowledge, memories, emotional states and environmental surroundings, allowing listeners to construct meaning through processes of association and imagination (Han, 2016; Margulis et al., 2019).
text.formatted: During music listening, experiences are shaped by prior knowledge, memories, emotional states and environmental surroundings, allowing listeners to construct meaning through processes of association and imagination <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Han, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Margulis et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Through these processes, listeners connect fragmented, perceptual, emotional, and contextual information to form meaningful internal representations and fill in temporal, spatial or logical gaps within their experience of the music (Fortuna & Nijs, 2020; Han, 2016).
text.formatted: Through these processes, listeners connect fragmented, perceptual, emotional, and contextual information to form meaningful internal representations and fill in temporal, spatial or logical gaps within their experience of the music <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Fortuna & Nijs, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Han, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, music can evoke semantic, narrative and multisensory information despite the absence of explicit linguistic or visual content (Groves et al., 2025; Jakubowski et al., 2024; Margulis, Williams, et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Consequently, music can evoke semantic, narrative and multisensory information despite the absence of explicit linguistic or visual content <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Groves et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Jakubowski et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Margulis, Williams, et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Such imagined scenarios may be voluntary and flexible (Curwen, 2025), ranging from autobiographical memories to fictional scenes (Margulis, Wong, et al., 2022), or involuntary and spontaneous, such as mind wandering and daydreaming during music listening (Taruffi, 2021).
text.formatted: Such imagined scenarios may be voluntary and flexible <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Curwen, 2025)</ref>, ranging from autobiographical memories to fictional scenes <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Margulis, Wong, et al., 2022)</ref>, or involuntary and spontaneous, such as mind wandering and daydreaming during music listening <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Taruffi, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: In the past decade, multiple studies have demonstrated that MEMI is a meaningful and recurring component of music listening rather than an isolated cognitive byproduct (Dahl et al., 2023; Herff et al., 2021; Taruffi et al., 2017).
text.formatted: In the past decade, multiple studies have demonstrated that MEMI is a meaningful and recurring component of music listening rather than an isolated cognitive byproduct <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Dahl et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Herff et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Taruffi et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Such experiences have been observed across a wide range of listening contexts, including personal music listening, task-irrelevant mind wandering and guided imagery paradigms (Herff et al., 2021; Taruffi, 2021; Taruffi et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Such experiences have been observed across a wide range of listening contexts, including personal music listening, task-irrelevant mind wandering and guided imagery paradigms <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Herff et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Taruffi, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Taruffi et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Similar phenomena have been reported across age groups ranging from children to older adults (Ayyildiz, Geibel, et al., 2025; Fortuna & Nijs, 2020; O'Shea et al., 2025; Owen et al., 2024), and across different cultural backgrounds (Loui et al., 2025; Margulis et al., 2019; Margulis, Wong, et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Similar phenomena have been reported across age groups ranging from children to older adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Ayyildiz, Geibel, et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Fortuna & Nijs, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">O'Shea et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Owen et al., 2024)</ref>, and across different cultural backgrounds <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Loui et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Margulis et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Margulis, Wong, et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these studies suggest that imagery experiences form a pervasive and ecologically relevant component of music perception, extending beyond laboratory settings into everyday listening experiences.
The significance of MEMI extends beyond music perception research.
Previous studies have demonstrated its relevance to cognitive, emotional, social and clinical domains.
Cognitive studies have associated MEMI with episodic memory, prospective thinking, creativity, imagination, and artistic expression (Taruffi & Küssner, 2019).
text.formatted: Cognitive studies have associated MEMI with episodic memory, prospective thinking, creativity, imagination, and artistic expression <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Taruffi & Küssner, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Emotionally, imagined content during music listening may influence aesthetic experiences and personal meaning-making through the interactions among memory, music, imagination and emotions (Fox & Beaty, 2019; Margulis & Jakubowski, 2024).
text.formatted: Emotionally, imagined content during music listening may influence aesthetic experiences and personal meaning-making through the interactions among memory, music, imagination and emotions <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Fox & Beaty, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Margulis & Jakubowski, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: From a social perspective, theories such as social surrogacy hypothesis, persona theory and simulation hypothesis highlight the role of music listening and imagery as a substitute for social interaction, confidence and confabulation of autobiographical memories (Herff et al., 2025; Jakubowski et al., 2024; Taruffi et al., 2023).
text.formatted: From a social perspective, theories such as social surrogacy hypothesis, persona theory and simulation hypothesis highlight the role of music listening and imagery as a substitute for social interaction, confidence and confabulation of autobiographical memories <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Herff et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Jakubowski et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Taruffi et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Clinically, imagery-based music therapies including the "Bonny Method of Guided Imagery and Music" (GIM; Bonny, 2002) illustrates its application in regulating anxiety, depression, stress, and overall wellbeing (Küssner & Eerola, 2019).
text.formatted: Clinically, imagery-based music therapies including the "Bonny Method of Guided Imagery and Music" (GIM; <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Bonny, 2002)</ref> illustrates its application in regulating anxiety, depression, stress, and overall wellbeing <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Küssner & Eerola, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: These perspectives position MEMI not as a singular or isolated phenomenon, but as a complex experience shaped by interacting sensory, emotional, cognitive and contextual processes.

Research on MEMI has employed a range of methods, including subjective ratings, questionnaires, thematic analyses, verbal descriptions, and behavioural paradigms (Herff et al., 2021; Margulis et al., 2019; O'Shea et al., 2025; Owen et al., 2024; Taruffi et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Research on MEMI has employed a range of methods, including subjective ratings, questionnaires, thematic analyses, verbal descriptions, and behavioural paradigms <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Herff et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Margulis et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">O'Shea et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Owen et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Taruffi et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: These approaches have provided valuable insights into different aspects of imagery, but they have often examined specific dimensions or outcomes separately.
Consequently, the relationships among the sensory, emotional, narrative, cognitive and contextual aspects of MEMI remain insufficiently understood.

Existing research has begun to address this challenge by developing conceptual frameworks for understanding MEMI and its associated processes (Taruffi & Küssner, 2019 , Küssner et al., 2022; Margulis & Jakubowski, 2024).
text.formatted: Existing research has begun to address this challenge by developing conceptual frameworks for understanding MEMI and its associated processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Taruffi & Küssner, 2019</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">, Küssner et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Margulis & Jakubowski, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: One approach is through bottom-up phenomenological characteristics of imagery, using measures such as vividness, prevalence, narrative engagement, emotional intensity, autobiographical memories, temporal unfolding and aesthetic judgement (Belfi, 2019; Herff et al., 2021; Jakubowski et al., 2024; Loui et al., 2025; Margulis et al., 2019; Margulis, Williams, et al., 2022; O'Shea et al., 2025).
text.formatted: One approach is through bottom-up phenomenological characteristics of imagery, using measures such as vividness, prevalence, narrative engagement, emotional intensity, autobiographical memories, temporal unfolding and aesthetic judgement <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Belfi, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Herff et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Jakubowski et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Loui et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Margulis et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Margulis, Williams, et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">O'Shea et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Another approach focuses directly on the descriptive and introspective aspects of imagery experiences, including imagined content, elements, themes, emotion categories and semantic space (Cowen et al., 2020; Dahl et al., 2023; Groves et al., 2025; Küssner & Eerola, 2019; Van Der Walle et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Another approach focuses directly on the descriptive and introspective aspects of imagery experiences, including imagined content, elements, themes, emotion categories and semantic space <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Cowen et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Dahl et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Groves et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Küssner & Eerola, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Van Der Walle et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: While attempts have been made to create scales that can systematically evaluate these dimensions, for example, the Narrativity Engagement (NE) Scale (Margulis et al., 2019), such approaches often remain restricted to standalone constructs of imagery, limiting a consolidated understanding of how these different characteristics co-occur within a common framework.

text.text: Another compelling aspect of MEMI is its multisensory and crossmodal nature.
While listening to music, a person may imagine bodily movement, gestures, or visual scenes that unfold alongside the musical beats (Taruffi & Küssner, 2019).
text.formatted: While listening to music, a person may imagine bodily movement, gestures, or visual scenes that unfold alongside the musical beats <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Taruffi & Küssner, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: These imagined representations can in turn shape auditory expectations and influence the broader musical experience (Nanay, 2022).
text.formatted: These imagined representations can in turn shape auditory expectations and influence the broader musical experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Nanay, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Although visual imagery has previous received considerable attention in MEMI research (Herff et al., 2021), imagery during music listening can involve auditory, motor, kinesthetic, tactile, olfactory, gustatory and synesthetic experiences (Küssner et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Although visual imagery has previous received considerable attention in MEMI research <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Herff et al., 2021)</ref>, imagery during music listening can involve auditory, motor, kinesthetic, tactile, olfactory, gustatory and synesthetic experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Küssner et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: These modalities involved, and the extent to which they are experienced, may vary with factors such as music genre, emotion expression, familiarity and liking of the music itself (Jakubowski et al., 2024).
text.formatted: These modalities involved, and the extent to which they are experienced, may vary with factors such as music genre, emotion expression, familiarity and liking of the music itself <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Jakubowski et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Capturing this range of experiences is therefore important for characterising the forms that MEMI can take.

Theoretical studies propose that imagery functions as one of the mechanisms through which music evokes emotions and mood (Juslin, 2013; Juslin & Västfjäll, 2008), while empirical studies indicate a more complex relationship between music, emotions, and imagery (O'Shea et al., 2025; Taruffi, 2021; Taruffi & Küssner, 2019).
text.formatted: Theoretical studies propose that imagery functions as one of the mechanisms through which music evokes emotions and mood <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Juslin, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Juslin & Västfjäll, 2008)</ref>, while empirical studies indicate a more complex relationship between music, emotions, and imagery <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(O'Shea et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Taruffi, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Taruffi & Küssner, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, previous research has provided strong evidence supporting emotional valence as an important predictor of MEMI (Belfi, 2019; Xu et al., 2025) shaping the content, vividness of scenes, movement-oriented imagery, including imagined dancing, and feelings of social connectedness during music listening (Belfi, 2019; Margulis et al., 2019; Taruffi et al., 2017; Taruffi & Küssner, 2019; Margulis & Jakubowski, 2024; Xu et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Nevertheless, previous research has provided strong evidence supporting emotional valence as an important predictor of MEMI <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Belfi, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Xu et al., 2025)</ref> shaping the content, vividness of scenes, movement-oriented imagery, including imagined dancing, and feelings of social connectedness during music listening <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Belfi, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Margulis et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Taruffi et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Taruffi & Küssner, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Margulis & Jakubowski, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Xu et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, the emotional quality expressed by music need not correspond to the emotion experienced by the listener or associated with the imagined content.
For instance, a music perceived as happy may evoke a positive memory from the past that elicits sadness (O'Shea et al., 2025; Taruffi et al., 2017).
text.formatted: For instance, a music perceived as happy may evoke a positive memory from the past that elicits sadness <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(O'Shea et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Taruffi et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Research distinguishing perceived musical emotion from felt emotion has therefore highlighted the complexity of emotional responses to music (Eerola & Vuoskoski, 2011), with models such as Geneva Emotional Music Scale (GEMS) and Geneva Music-Induced Affect Checklist (GEMIAC) capturing a broader range of musical emotions than valence and arousal alone (Coutinho & Scherer, 2017; Zentner et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Research distinguishing perceived musical emotion from felt emotion has therefore highlighted the complexity of emotional responses to music <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Eerola & Vuoskoski, 2011)</ref>, with models such as Geneva Emotional Music Scale (GEMS) and Geneva Music-Induced Affect Checklist (GEMIAC) capturing a broader range of musical emotions than valence and arousal alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Coutinho & Scherer, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Zentner et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Imageryrelated emotions may likewise overlap with narrative and semantic characteristics of imagined content (Cowen et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Imageryrelated emotions may likewise overlap with narrative and semantic characteristics of imagined content <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Cowen et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Such findings motivate examining emotional experience alongside, rather than as a substitute for, other characteristics of MEMI.
MEMI is substantially heterogeneous and idiosyncratic in nature (Curwen, 2025; Dahl et al., 2023; Hashim et al., 2023; Küssner & Eerola, 2019).
text.formatted: MEMI is substantially heterogeneous and idiosyncratic in nature <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Curwen, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Dahl et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Hashim et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Küssner & Eerola, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Prior sensory experiences, personal memories, cultural background, education, and language may influence how listeners interpret music and construct imagery (Owen et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Prior sensory experiences, personal memories, cultural background, education, and language may influence how listeners interpret music and construct imagery <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Owen et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Immediate environment and associated mental states may further influence the frequency and content of imagined thoughts (Margulis & Jakubowski, 2024).
text.formatted: Immediate environment and associated mental states may further influence the frequency and content of imagined thoughts <ref type="bibr">(Margulis & Jakubowski, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, the same musical excerpt can evoke different narratives and semantic associations across listeners (Herff et al., 2021; Taruffi et al., 2023; Van Der Walle et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Consequently, the same musical excerpt can evoke different narratives and semantic associations across listeners <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Herff et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Taruffi et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Van Der Walle et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Narrative engagement, for example, may be high even when listeners disagree about the stories they imagine (Margulis, Wong, et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Narrative engagement, for example, may be high even when listeners disagree about the stories they imagine <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Margulis, Wong, et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Familiarity and liking may also influence the frequency and character of music-related thoughts, although their effects on the novelty of imagined content may differ (Jakubowski et al., 2024; Van Der Walle et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Familiarity and liking may also influence the frequency and character of music-related thoughts, although their effects on the novelty of imagined content may differ <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Jakubowski et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Van Der Walle et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond these contextual and appraisal-related factors, musical expertise, listening habits, reward sensitivity, creative identity, controllability, and individual imagery ability may contribute to differences in how people engage with music (Beaty et al., 2013; Belfi, 2019; Groves et al., 2025; Jakubowski et al., 2024; Taruffi & Küssner, 2019; Ayyildiz, Milne, et al., 2025; Küssner et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Beyond these contextual and appraisal-related factors, musical expertise, listening habits, reward sensitivity, creative identity, controllability, and individual imagery ability may contribute to differences in how people engage with music <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Beaty et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Belfi, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Groves et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Jakubowski et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Taruffi & Küssner, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Ayyildiz, Milne, et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Küssner et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Such variability is not merely a source of methodological noise within MEMI research, but rather a defining characteristic of how imagery experiences emerge and acquire meaning to the music.

Although imagery experiences are inherently shaped by the listener, the acoustic and structural properties of the music also influence the content and characteristics of imagined experiences (Margulis & Jakubowski, 2024).
text.formatted: Although imagery experiences are inherently shaped by the listener, the acoustic and structural properties of the music also influence the content and characteristics of imagined experiences <ref type="bibr">(Margulis & Jakubowski, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Instrumental music can evoke rich extra-musical concepts and semantic associations despite the absence of explicit visual or linguistic information (Groves et al., 2025; Margulis, Williams, et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Instrumental music can evoke rich extra-musical concepts and semantic associations despite the absence of explicit visual or linguistic information <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Groves et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Margulis, Williams, et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: As music unfolds over time, changes in rhythm, timbre, harmony, tempo, and musical tension can shape varieties of temporal progression, emotional tone, vividness, and narrative development of imagined events (Margulis, Wong, et al., 2022).
text.formatted: As music unfolds over time, changes in rhythm, timbre, harmony, tempo, and musical tension can shape varieties of temporal progression, emotional tone, vividness, and narrative development of imagined events <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Margulis, Wong, et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Acoustic features such as pitch, loudness and tempo have been associated with specific forms of imagery, including motor simulations, spatial characteristics, and imagined fictitious scenes (Groves et al., 2025; Herff et al., 2021; Margulis, Williams, et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Acoustic features such as pitch, loudness and tempo have been associated with specific forms of imagery, including motor simulations, spatial characteristics, and imagined fictitious scenes <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Groves et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Herff et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Margulis, Williams, et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Even subtle performance characteristics, such as microvariations in timing, pitch, and timbre, have been shown to enhance imagery vividness, immersion, and perceived movement (Ayyildiz, Milne, et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Even subtle performance characteristics, such as microvariations in timing, pitch, and timbre, have been shown to enhance imagery vividness, immersion, and perceived movement <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Ayyildiz, Milne, et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, much of this work has examined specific acoustic features or imagery outcomes using a limited set of musical excerpts.
How broader combinations of acoustic characteristics relate to the multiple dimensions of MEMI therefore remains an important question.
The multidimensional nature of MEMI highlights that the selection of musical stimuli is not merely a methodological consideration but a theoretical one.

If imagery experiences are shaped by emotional expression, narrative affordances, acoustic structure, familiarity, cultural associations, and individual listener characteristics, then the choice of musical excerpts fundamentally determines the forms of imagery that can be observed and investigated (Cowen et al., 2020; Dahl et al., 2023; Herff et al., 2021; Loui et al., 2025; Margulis et al., 2019; Margulis, Wong, et al., 2022).
text.formatted: If imagery experiences are shaped by emotional expression, narrative affordances, acoustic structure, familiarity, cultural associations, and individual listener characteristics, then the choice of musical excerpts fundamentally determines the forms of imagery that can be observed and investigated <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Cowen et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Dahl et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Herff et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Loui et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Margulis et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Margulis, Wong, et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: To date, however, most MEMI studies have selected musical stimuli to address specific experimental questions, typically relying on relatively small, ad hoc collections of musical excerpts.

While such stimulus selection is appropriate for hypothesis-driven investigations, it makes the direct comparisons across studies difficult and limits the accumulation of normative knowledge about the imagery characteristics of individual musical excerpts.

As a result, it remains unclear whether differences in reported imagery reflect genuine properties of MEMI or simply arise from variation in the musical stimuli employed across studies, limiting reproducibility and cumulative theory building within the field.
Several standardised musical stimulus databases have been developed to facilitate research in music perception, cognition and emotion.

For example, Taste and Affect Music Database (Guedes et al., 2023) which investigates taste correspondences and affective responses of instrumental music; the Famous Melodies Stimulus Set (Belfi & Kacirek, 2021), developed to investigate musical familiarity and namerecall ability; music stimulus sets normed for perceived and/or felt emotion responses (Eerola & Vuoskoski, 2011; Strauss et al., 2024); and the Previously Used Musical Stimuli dataset (PUMS; Warrenburg, 2021), which catalogues musical stimuli used across decades of music psychology research.
text.formatted: For example, Taste and Affect Music Database <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Guedes et al., 2023)</ref> which investigates taste correspondences and affective responses of instrumental music; the Famous Melodies Stimulus Set <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Belfi & Kacirek, 2021)</ref>, developed to investigate musical familiarity and namerecall ability; music stimulus sets normed for perceived and/or felt emotion responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Eerola & Vuoskoski, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Strauss et al., 2024)</ref>; and the Previously Used Musical Stimuli dataset (PUMS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Warrenburg, 2021)</ref>, which catalogues musical stimuli used across decades of music psychology research.

text.text: Among the resources most relevant to MEMI research are the Narrative Engagement Stimulus (NES) dataset, which provides musical excerpts normed for their capacity to elicit narrative engagement among Western and Chinese listeners (Loui et al., 2025; Margulis et al., 2019) and MUSIFEAST-17 (Van Der Walle et al., 2025), which extends stimulus characterisation by incorporating ratings of familiarity, enjoyment, contextual associations, and music-evoked thoughts across a diverse range of musical genres.
text.formatted: Among the resources most relevant to MEMI research are the Narrative Engagement Stimulus (NES) dataset, which provides musical excerpts normed for their capacity to elicit narrative engagement among Western and Chinese listeners <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Loui et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Margulis et al., 2019)</ref> and <ref type="bibr">MUSIFEAST-17 (Van Der Walle et al., 2025)</ref>, which extends stimulus characterisation by incorporating ratings of familiarity, enjoyment, contextual associations, and music-evoked thoughts across a diverse range of musical genres.

text.text: Collectively, these resources demonstrate the value of characterising musical stimuli across multiple dimensions of listener experience.

However, their primary focus remains on individual dimensions, rather than the multidimensional experiences across the occurrence, phenomenological characteristics and representational content of MEMI.

To our knowledge, no existing musical stimulus resource integrates ratings of imagery phenomenology, sensory modalities, imagined content, imagery-related emotional associations, and acoustic characteristics within a single database.

A multidimensional, open-access resource of this kind would allow researchers to select musical excerpts according to their imagery profiles and provide a shared basis for investigating how musical, psychological and phenomenological characteristics relate to MEMI.

The primary aim of the present study was to develop and characterise MUSIMAGINE, an open-access database of musical excerpts accompanied by multidimensional measures of music-evoked mental imagery (MEMI).

The database was designed to address the need for a shared resource for MEMI research by providing stimuli-level information on imagery occurrence, phenomenological characteristics, representational content, subjective music appraisals, and acoustic properties.
By making these measures available together, MUSIMAGINE aims to support more reproducible and comparable investigations of MEMI.
In addition to developing the database, the study addressed two further objectives.
First, we characterised imagery experiences by examining their occurrence, phenomenological ratings, reported representational content, and participants' free-text descriptions.

Second, we investigated the factors associated with imagery occurrence by examining the contribution of listeners' subjective evaluations of the music, individual differences in imagery ability and musical background, and the acoustic properties of the musical excerpts.

These analyses provide an initial empirical characterisation of the database and illustrate how it can be used to investigate relationships between musical stimuli, listener characteristics, and MEMI.
>Method
text.formatted: <head n="4." >Method</head>

text.text: A total of 153 participants (65 females, 87 males, and 1 preferred not to say) completed the online experiment.
Participants were recruited through Prolific.

The sample comprised participants across a broad age range, with 32.7% aged 18-24 years, 41.8% aged 25-34 years, 20.9% aged 35-44 years, 1.9% aged 45-54 years, 1.9% aged 55-64 years, and 0.6% aged 65 years or older.
The majority of participants (97.4%) reported normal hearing.
Four participants reported a known hearing impairment.

As hearing ability was not specified as an eligibility criterion during recruitment, and preliminary sensitivity analyses with these participants excluded did not indicate any substantive changes in the results, these participants were retained for subsequent analyses.

Participants represented 35 countries of origin, were residing in 27 different countries at the time of testing, and reported 31 native languages, reflecting a geographically and linguistically diverse international sample.
The largest country-of-origin group was Egypt (19.6%), while English was the most commonly reported native language (42.5%).

Participants also reported a broad range of musical training, with 32.7% reporting no formal musical training, 13.7% reporting 0.5 years, 10.4% reporting 1 year, 19.6% reporting 2 years, 15.0% reporting 3-5 years, 5.2% reporting 6-9 years, and 3.3% reporting 10 or more years of formal musical training.
All participants provided informed consent prior to participation.
The study was approved by the University of Jyväskylä Ethics Committee, and all methods were carried out in accordance with relevant guidelines and regulations as approved by the JYU IRB.
The stimulus set consisted of 60 self-selected music excerpts from an open-source music repository (https://pixabay.com/music/).
text.formatted: The stimulus set consisted of 60 self-selected music excerpts from an open-source music repository (<ref type="url" target="https://pixabay.com/music/">https://pixabay.com/music/</ref>).

text.text: The inclusion criteria specified that clips should be at least 60s long, with no lyrics.
The music excerpts were verified to be non-AI-generated and labelled copyright-free, permitting their use and redistribution within an open research context.
The instrumental music was selected to maximise acoustic variability and elicit diverse imagery content.
To achieve this, the music pieces were selected across different 'Genre', 'Mood', 'Movement' and 'Theme' as categorised on the Pixabay database.
The excerpts were selected to build a stimulus set where different emotion quadrants on the two-dimensional valence-arousal space are represented (Russell, 1980).
text.formatted: The excerpts were selected to build a stimulus set where different emotion quadrants on the two-dimensional valence-arousal space are represented <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Russell, 1980)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, 15 music excerpts were assigned to each quadrant: High Valence-High Arousal (HVHA), High Valence-Low Arousal (HVLA), Low Valence-High Arousal (LVHA) and Low Valence-Low Arousal (LVLA), based on researcher judgment informed by perceived emotional content.
This classification was used as an initial heuristic for the study and was empirically validated during the experiment.
To minimize familiarity and likability effects, the music was selected ensuring that they are not commercially popular or easily recognisable.
However, these variables were not explicitly controlled and were assessed through participant ratings during the experiment.

Longer music excerpts were trimmed to 60s in length (sampling rate = 44100 Hz, stereo, .mp3 files) and a 500ms fade-in and fade-out was added in the beginning and end of each audio clip using Audacity.
No additional processing was applied, as preserving natural acoustic variation was important for capturing differences in imagery responses.

All clips are available under educational use and fair use of academic research and are made available as part of an open-access stimulus set in the MUSIMAGINE repository: https://osf.io/z2kry/overview?view_only=bcd3ff22b3624132b2e3bddd22e85548.

text.text: The study questions were compiled into a questionnaire implemented using jsPsych and hosted on the JATOS server (see https://osf.io/z2kry/overview?view_only=bcd3ff22b3624132b2e3bddd22e85548kry/) (Lange et al., 2015; Leeuw et al., 2023).

text.text: After each 60s music stimulus, participants responded to a question assessing imagery presence, with a binary response (Yes/No) (Fig. 1).
text.formatted: After each 60s music stimulus, participants responded to a question assessing imagery presence, with a binary response (Yes/No) (Fig. <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: Based on this response, a conditional branching structure was implemented to assess further aspects of imagery.

If participants responded 'Yes' to the imagery presence question for that stimulus, they were asked to rate multiple dimensions of imagery on a 0-100 visual analogue scale including ease, vividness, clarity, narrativity, movement, and emotion intensity presented in a randomized order.
Each scale was anchored from low to high corresponding to the respective dimensions.
Further, participants were asked to respond to multiple choice questions assessing different characteristics of their imagery experience.
Participants were allowed to select multiple options for each of the above categories.

These included: Types of imagery content: these included elements to capture the descriptive overview of the broader content of the experience distinguishing between people, place, actions, yourself/self-referential, autobiographical memories, objects, abstract, and others.
These describe a non-exhaustive list of what appears in the imagery.

Imagery Questionnaire (Andrade et al., 2014) used to assess imagery vividness across sensory domains including, visual, auditory, tactile/somatosensory, interoceptive, affective, olfactory, gustatory imagery.
text.formatted: Imagery Questionnaire <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Andrade et al., 2014)</ref> used to assess imagery vividness across sensory domains including, visual, auditory, tactile/somatosensory, interoceptive, affective, olfactory, gustatory imagery.

text.text: Motor and kinesthetic imagery along with others were included to capture movement-related experiences.

Emotional content of imagery: assessed using categories derived from the Geneva Emotional Music Scale (GEMS; Zentner et al., 2008) and the extended categories of Geneva Music-Induced Affect Checklist (GEMIAC; Coutinho & Scherer, 2017).
text.formatted: Emotional content of imagery: assessed using categories derived from the Geneva Emotional Music Scale (GEMS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Zentner et al., 2008)</ref> and the extended categories of Geneva Music-Induced Affect Checklist (GEMIAC; <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Coutinho & Scherer, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, two further emotion categories (mysterious/uncanny and scary/fearful) were included, along with none/unclear, others.
Beyond this, participants were also asked to provide a free-text description of their imagery experience, allowing for qualitative insights into imagery content.

In cases where participants responded 'No' to the imagery presence question, they were instead asked to rate the ease of generating imagery and the potential for imagery when guided (e.g., imagining a visual scene) using 0-100 slider scales.
They were additionally asked to indicate reasons for the absence of imagery and elements that might facilitate imagery for the given music using multiplechoice (select all that apply) questions.
A free-text response was also collected to describe the reason for the absence of imagery.

Regardless of imagery presence, all participants provided subjective music appraisal ratings for each stimulus, including valence (unpleasant-pleasant), arousal (calm-energising), liking and familiarity using continuous slider scales from 0-100.
Following the main experimental task, participants completed a set of questionnaires assessing individual differences relevant to imagery and music processing.
These included a shortened Plymouth Sensory Imagery Questionnaire (PSIQ; Andrade et al., 2014), used to assess subjective imagery ability across sensory modalities.
text.formatted: These included a shortened Plymouth Sensory Imagery Questionnaire (PSIQ; <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Andrade et al., 2014)</ref>, used to assess subjective imagery ability across sensory modalities.

text.text: Two items were randomly selected for each modality, and responses were collected using a 0-10 continuous slider scale.
Additionally, two items were adapted from the Goldsmiths Musical Sophistication Index (Gold-MSI; Müllensiefen et al., 2014), assessing music-related activities and formal musical training.
text.formatted: Additionally, two items were adapted from the Goldsmiths Musical Sophistication Index (Gold-MSI; <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Müllensiefen et al., 2014)</ref>, assessing music-related activities and formal musical training.

text.text: Three items were adapted from the Barcelona Music Reward Questionnaire (BMRQ; Mas-Herrero et al., 2013), assessing emotional responsiveness to music, engagement to new music and bodily movement in response to music.
text.formatted: Three items were adapted from the Barcelona Music Reward Questionnaire (BMRQ; <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Mas-Herrero et al., 2013)</ref>, assessing emotional responsiveness to music, engagement to new music and bodily movement in response to music.

text.text: Further, two self-developed items were included to assess music-related mind wandering and music association tendencies.
These items were presented as radio-button responses on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from "completely disagree" to "completely agree".
Finally, participants completed a set of demographic questions, including age, gender, hearing status, current country of residence, country of origin and native language.
In addition, participants were asked to report up to two music pieces that they believed effectively elicited mental imagery during listening.
Overview of the experimental paradigm
The experiment was conducted online, allowing participants to complete the study from their own setting.
The 60 music clips were counterbalanced across the participants and only a subset of 12 music stimuli (3 from each emotion quadrant) were presented to each participant.
The subset selection ensured that each participant was exposed to stimuli from all four emotions quadrant equally.
The target sample size was determined to ensure that each stimulus was evaluated by at least 30 participants (range = 30-34) (Strauss et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The target sample size was determined to ensure that each stimulus was evaluated by at least 30 participants (range = 30-34) <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Strauss et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Participants were first presented with an information sheet explaining the study and were asked to confirm their informed consent to participate in the study.
Participants were instructed to conduct the experiment alone in a quiet environment, preferably with headphones to avoid distractions.
Participants then listened to 12 music clips in a random order.
Each trial consisted of the presentation of a single 60s music excerpt, during which participants were instructed to listen attentively.
Playback proceeded for the full duration of the clip without interruption.
Participants were not allowed to pause, replay or skip the audio clips.

After each clip, the screen automatically progressed to present them with the question on imagery presence, followed by conditionally presented (bifurcated) imagery related questions based on their previous response and the general questions about the music.
All responses were self-paced.
After listening and responding to all 12 music clips, participants completed questions on the individual traits of sensory imagery, musical background and demographics questions.
These questionnaires were administered after the main task to avoid influencing trial-by-trial responses.
The total duration of the experiment was 30-40 minutes.
Finally, the participants were reimbursed for their time after the task was completed.
To characterise the acoustic properties of the music excerpts, acoustic features were extracted from all 60 stimuli using the MIRToolbox (v.
1.8.1) (Lartillot et al., 2008) in MATLAB.
text.formatted: 1.8.1) <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Lartillot et al., 2008)</ref> in MATLAB.

text.text: Feature extraction was performed on the WAV files of the musical excerpts.
Most descriptors were extracted using the mirfeatures function (frame length: 0.2s), while pulse clarity (frame length: 5s) and event density (frame length: 10s) were extracted separately.
The initial extraction yielded 263 feature variables.
Features containing only missing values or exhibiting no variability across the stimulus set were excluded from further analyses.

From the resulting candidate feature set, 54 features were selected to provide coverage of multiple acoustic domains, including dynamics, fluctuation, rhythm, spectral and cepstral characteristics, timbre and tonal properties informed by previous music information retrieval research (Eerola, 2011).
text.formatted: From the resulting candidate feature set, 54 features were selected to provide coverage of multiple acoustic domains, including dynamics, fluctuation, rhythm, spectral and cepstral characteristics, timbre and tonal properties informed by previous music information retrieval research <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Eerola, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: The final selection of feature set retained summary statistics across complementary acoustic dimensions (means, standard deviations, and slope, where applicable) and included the means of 13 mel-frequency cepstral coefficient (MFCCs).
All 54 selected features were standardised using z-score normalisation before subsequent statistical analyses.
The extracted acoustic features and the extraction code are available in the MUSIMAGINE repository: https://osf.io/z2kry/overview?view_only=bcd3ff22b3624132b2e3bddd22e85548.
text.formatted: The extracted acoustic features and the extraction code are available in the MUSIMAGINE repository: <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/z2kry/overview?view_only=bcd3ff22b3624132b2e3bddd22e85548">https://osf.io/z2kry/</ref>.

text.text: All analyses were conducted in R (v.
Responses were screened for completeness prior to analysis.

Trials in which participants did not report experiencing mental imagery were retained for analyses of imagery occurrence but excluded from analyses of imagery characteristics and open-ended descriptions.
Open-ended responses provided in language other than English by one participant were translated using DeepL prior to analysis.
One response containing no meaningful description was excluded from the text-based analyses.

The analytical strategy was designed to address three complementary objectives: 1) validation of the stimulus database, 2) characterisation of MEMI elicited by the musical excerpts, and 3) identification of factors associated with MEMI.
Database validation focused on the intended emotional categorisation of the excerpts and the reliability of participants' ratings.
Characterisation analyses summarised the prevalence, dimensions, phenomenological properties, and descriptive characteristics of imagery experiences elicited by the stimulus set.
Predictor analyses examined the contribution of listeners' subjective evaluations, participant characteristics, and acoustic features to the occurrence of MEMI.
Continuous variables were summarised using descriptive statistics (M, SD, and range), whereas categorical variables were summarised using frequencies and percentages.
Statistical significance was set at p < .05 for all analyses.
text.formatted: Statistical significance was set at p < .05 for all analyses.

text.text: Associations between continuous variables were examined using Pearson correlation coefficients.
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was performed on stimulus-level mean imagery dimension ratings to explore the underlying structure of these six imagery dimensions.

Specific to the analysis of acoustic descriptors, pairwise Pearson correlations were examined to characterise relationships among the selected descriptors and assess the degree of redundancy within the feature set.
PCA was then performed on the standardised acoustic descriptors to reduce the dimensionality of the acoustic feature space.

The number of components retained for further analysis was determined using Horn's parallel analysis and subjected to oblimin rotation to improve interpretability among the latent acoustic dimensions.
Component scores for each musical excerpt were extracted and used as predictors in subsequent mixed-effects models.

Owing to the repeated-measures design of the study, in which each participant rated multiple musical excerpts and each excerpt was evaluated by multiple participants, linear and generalised mixed-effects models (lme4 package) were used to account for the non-independence of observations by including participant and stimulus as random intercepts.

Generalised linear mixed-effects models with a binomial error distribution were used to analyse imagery occurrence, whereas linear mixed-effects models were used for imagery dimension and other continuous variables.

Model improvement was assessed using likelihood ratio tests comparing fitted models with corresponding null models and the significance of individual predictors was evaluated using Type III Wald χ² tests or F tests, as appropriate.
Marginal and conditional R² values were calculated to quantify the variance explained by the mixedeffects models.

For analyses involving categorical predictors with more than two levels, significant effects were followed by post hoc pairwise comparisons using estimated marginal means (emmeans package) with Holm correction for multiple comparisons.

For the multi-response measures, the consistency of imagery responses across listeners was quantified using Shannon entropy calculated from the combinations of imagery elements, sensory modalities, and imagery-associated emotions selected for each musical excerpt.
Open-text imagery descriptions were characterised using response length (word count), lexical concreteness, and lexical-semantic convergence.
Lexical concreteness was quantified using the word-level concreteness norms (Brysbaert et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Lexical concreteness was quantified using the word-level concreteness norms <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Brysbaert et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Each description was tokenised into individual words, which were matched to the norms, and a mean concreteness score was calculated for each description by averaging the ratings of matched words.
Words without corresponding norm ratings were excluded from this calculation.
Lexical-semantic convergence was assessed by analysing the lexical similarity of participants' opentext imagery descriptions.
Missing, empty, and placeholder responses were excluded.
The remaining descriptions were tokenised into individual words, and English stop words, task-related terms, and numeric-only tokens were removed.
Words were lemmatised to consolidate inflected norms.
To ensure sufficient lexical content for similarity estimation, descriptions were required to contain at least three tokens after preprocessing.
Words occurring only once across the eligible descriptions were then excluded, and the minimum three-token criterion was reapplied.
Each description was then represented as a TF-IDF weighted lexical vector and pairwise cosine similarity was calculated between descriptions.
Mean pairwise similarity was calculated for each musical excerpt to quantify withinstimulus lexical-semantic convergence.

To assess whether this convergence exceeded chance expectations, a participant-stratified permutation was conducted in which stimulus identities were randomly reassigned among descriptions within each participant while the lexical similarity matrix was held constant.
The observed mean within-stimulus similarity was compared with the resulting permutation distribution.
Analyses were conducted at both the participant-level and the stimulus level, depending on the question being addressed.

Participant-level analyses were used to examine imagery occurrence and its predictors, whereas stimulus-level analyses were used to validate the database and characterise the imagery elicited by each musical excerpt.

The complete datasets used for both levels of analyses, together with the analysis scripts, are publicly available through the MUSIMAGINE repository: https://osf.io/z2kry/overview?view_only=bcd3ff22b3624132b2e3bddd22e85548.
text.formatted: The complete datasets used for both levels of analyses, together with the analysis scripts, are publicly available through the MUSIMAGINE repository: <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/z2kry/overview?view_only=bcd3ff22b3624132b2e3bddd22e85548">https://osf.io/z2kry/</ref>.

text.text: To validate the emotional characteristics of the stimulus set, participants rated the perceived valence and arousal of each music excerpt using continuous rating scales ranging from 0 to 100.
Each of the 60 excerpts received ratings from 30-34 participants.
Across all stimuli, mean valence ratings ranged from 41.7 to 83.5 (M = 66.9, SD = 26.6), whereas mean arousal ratings ranged from 29.3 to 83.1 (M = 55.5, SD = 30.6) (Fig. 2).
text.formatted: Across all stimuli, mean valence ratings ranged from 41.7 to 83.5 (M = 66.9, SD = 26.6), whereas mean arousal ratings ranged from 29.3 to 83.1 (M = 55.5, SD = 30.6) (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">2</ref>).

text.text: As intended, excerpts assigned to the high-valence categories received higher valence ratings (HVHA: M = 72.0, SD = 6.8; HVLA: M = 74.7, SD = 4.6) than those assigned to the lowvalence categories (LVHA: M = 58.6, SD = 8.6; LVLA: M = 62.1, SD = 6.5).

Similarly, excerpts assigned to high-arousal categories received higher arousal ratings (HVHA: M = 62.9, SD = 7.8; LVHA: M = 72.4, SD = 8.6) than those assigned to the low-arousal categories (HVLA: M = 42.5, SD = 8.1; LVLA: M = 44.5, SD = 9.3).
The consistency of the emotional ratings was assessed by examining the variability of valence and arousal ratings within each music excerpt.
Across the stimulus set, the average within-stimulus standard deviation was 25.1 for valence and 26.7 for arousal.
All stimuli exhibited consistent level of agreement, with no excerpt exceeding a z-score of 2.5 for the average within-stimulus standard deviation.
The observed variability therefore did not warrant the exclusion of any stimulus from the database.

The correspondence between the intended emotional categorisation and participants perceived emotional ratings was further examined by assigning an observed emotion label to each excerpt based on whether its mean valence and arousal ratings fell above or below the overall mean ratings of the stimulus set.

Comparison of the intended and participant-derived classifications showed that 41 of the 60 excerpts (68.3%) remained within their originally assigned emotional quadrant, whereas 19 excerpts (31.7%) were reclassified into neighbouring quadrants.
Most reclassifications involved shifts along a single emotional dimension, with relatively few excerpts shifting across both valence and arousal dimensions simultaneously.
Lastly, we examined whether the intended emotional categorisation reliably predicted participants' emotional evaluations.

Linear mixed-effects models were fitted to the participant-level valence and arousal ratings with intended emotion category as a fixed effect and participant and stimulus as random intercepts (general_valence/general_arousal ~ emotion_label + (1|participant) + (1|stimulus_id)).
Results show that the intended emotion category significantly predicted perceived valence (F(3, 52.88) = 23.39, η² = 0.57, p < .001).
text.formatted: Results show that the intended emotion category significantly predicted perceived valence (F(3, 52.88) = 23.39, η² = 0.57, p < .001).

text.text: Pairwise comparisons indicated that both high-valence categories (HVHA and HVLA) received significantly higher valence ratings than the two low-valence categories (LVHA and LVLA; all p-values < .001), whereas no significant differences were observed within the high-or low-valence pairs (both p-values > .05).
text.formatted: Pairwise comparisons indicated that both high-valence categories (HVHA and HVLA) received significantly higher valence ratings than the two low-valence categories (LVHA and LVLA; all p-values < .001), whereas no significant differences were observed within the high-or low-valence pairs (both p-values > .05).

text.text: Similarly, emotion category significantly predicted perceived arousal (F(3, 54.15) = 48.59, η² = 0.73, p < .001).
text.formatted: Similarly, emotion category significantly predicted perceived arousal (F(3, 54.15) = 48.59, η² = 0.73, p < .001).

text.text: Pairwise comparisons showed that the two low -arousal categories (HVLA and LVLA) did not differ significantly in perceived arousal (p > .05), whereas all remaining pairwise comparisons were statistically significant (all p-values < .01).
text.formatted: Pairwise comparisons showed that the two low -arousal categories (HVLA and LVLA) did not differ significantly in perceived arousal (p > .05), whereas all remaining pairwise comparisons were statistically significant (all p-values < .01).

text.text: These findings validate the emotional characteristics of the stimulus set and were therefore retained for all subsequent categorical analyses.
Our first objective was to examine whether the music excerpts in the stimulus dataset reliably evoked mental imagery across listeners.
Across all trials, participants reported experiencing mental imagery on 81.8% of listening trials.
At the stimulus level, imagery occurrence ranged from 51.6% to 100% (Fig. 3).
text.formatted: At the stimulus level, imagery occurrence ranged from 51.6% to 100% (Fig. <ref type="figure">3</ref>).

text.text: The distribution of imagery rates varied continuously across the stimulus set, with no clear separation between highly imagery-evoking and less imagery-evoking excerpts, suggesting that imagery occurrence existed along a continuum rather than as a binary property.
Observed imagery rates were similarly high across the four intended emotion categories (HVHA: 82.2%, HVLA: 82.2%, LVHA: 80.9%, LVLA: 81.9%).

Further, to determine whether imagery occurrence differed according to the intended emotional categorisation of the stimuli, a generalised linear mixed effects model with binomial error distribution was fitted using imagery presence as the dependent variable, intended emotion category as a fixed effect, and participant and stimulus as random intercepts.

Adding emotion category did not significantly improve the model fit relative to the null model (χ²(3) = 0.29, p = 0.96), indicating that the likelihood of reporting mental imagery did not differ across the four intended emotion categories.
The analysis was repeated using the observed emotion categories derived from participant-rated valence and arousal.
Observed emotion category did not significantly improve model fit relative to the null model (χ²(3) = 2.89, p = 0.41).

Pairwise comparisons likewise revealed no significant differences between the categories (all adjusted p-values = 1.00) for both analyses indicating that music-evoked mental imagery was prevalent across the database irrespective of the emotional categorisation of the stimuli.

Our next objective was to characterise the subjective qualities of the reported imagery.
Participants who reported experiencing mental imagery rated six dimensions of their experience using continuous rating scales ranging from 0 to 100 (Fig. 3).
text.formatted: Participants who reported experiencing mental imagery rated six dimensions of their experience using continuous rating scales ranging from 0 to 100 (Fig. <ref type="figure">3</ref>).

text.text: Descriptive statistics for all the imagery dimensions are presented in Table 1.
text.formatted: Descriptive statistics for all the imagery dimensions are presented in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>.

text.text: Overall, participants reported imagery that was generally easy to generate and characterised by relatively high levels of vividness, clarity, and narrativity.
Perceived movement and emotion intensity received comparatively lower ratings, although all dimensions exhibited substantial variability across participants and stimuli.
Pearson correlation coefficients were calculated between the mean ratings of the six imagery dimensions across the stimulus set (Fig. 4).
text.formatted: Pearson correlation coefficients were calculated between the mean ratings of the six imagery dimensions across the stimulus set (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">4</ref>).

text.text: Moderate to strong positive associations were observed among the imagery dimensions, indicating that music excerpts that evoked imagery which were easier to generate also tended to evoke imagery that was more vivid, clearer, and narrative.

In contrast, perceived movement exhibited comparatively weaker associations with the remaining imagery dimensions, while emotion intensity showed significant associations with vividness, clarity and narrativity but was not significantly associated with ease or perceived movement.
Across stimuli, mean within-stimulus SDs ranged from 23.05 to 26.27 points across the six dimensions.
Therefore, to investigate the underlying structure of the six imagery dimensions, a principal component analysis (PCA) was performed on the stimulus-level mean ratings.
PC1 accounted for 59.6% of the total variance, while the first two components (PC1+PC2) together explained 76.6% of the variance.
Ease, vividness, clarity, and narrativity loaded strongly on PC1, suggesting that these dimensions reflect a common underlying aspect of imagery quality.
In contrast, movement and emotion intensity contributed more strongly to PC2, indicating that these characteristics captured additional variation beyond the general imagery quality dimensions.
Finally, we examined whether these subjective characteristics of MEMI differed according to the emotional category of the music excerpts.

Separate linear mixed-effects models were fitted for each imagery dimension, with intended emotion category as a fixed effect and participant and stimulus as random intercepts (imagery_dimension ~ emotion_label + (1|participant) + ( 1|stimulus_id)).
