text.text: Intended emotion category did not significantly predict ratings of imagery ease, vividness, clarity, or narrativity (all p-values > .05; Table 1).
text.formatted: Intended emotion category did not significantly predict ratings of imagery ease, vividness, clarity, or narrativity (all p-values > .05; Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: On the contrary, perceived movement and emotion intensity differed significantly across emotion categories (Table 1).
text.formatted: On the contrary, perceived movement and emotion intensity differed significantly across emotion categories (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Pairwise comparisons indicated that both higharousal categories (HVHA and LVHA) received significantly higher movement ratings than the two lowarousal categories (HVLA and LVLA) (all adjusted p-values < .001), while no significant differences were observed within the high-or low-arousal category pairs.
text.formatted: Pairwise comparisons indicated that both higharousal categories (HVHA and LVHA) received significantly higher movement ratings than the two lowarousal categories (HVLA and LVLA) (all adjusted p-values < .001), while no significant differences were observed within the high-or low-arousal category pairs.

text.text: Likewise, pairwise comparisons showed that both low-valence categories (LVHA and LVLA) received significantly higher emotion intensity ratings than the two high-valence categories (HVHA and HVLA) (all adjusted p-values < .05), with no significant differences observed within either valence level.

The next objective was to further characterise the content and consistency of MEMI.
Participants reported the elements present in their mental images, the sensory modalities involved, and the emotions associated with those experiences.

To provide a comprehensive characterisation of the imagery elicited by the stimulus set, we examined the prevalence of individual response options together with the diversity of imagery experiences evoked by each musical excerpt.
The overall prevalence of imagery elements, sensory modalities, and imagery-associated emotions is presented in Fig. 5.
text.formatted: The overall prevalence of imagery elements, sensory modalities, and imagery-associated emotions is presented in Fig. <ref type="figure">5</ref>.

text.text: Percentages represent the proportion of imagery reports in which each response option was selected and therefore do not sum to 100%, as participants could select multiple responses.
Considerable variability was observed in the frequency with which individual response options were selected.
Among imagery elements, the most frequently reported were People (61.5%), Place (60.9%) and Actions (58.7%), whereas Memories (24%) and Abstracts (14.8%) were comparatively uncommon.
Across sensory modalities, Visual (66.8%) and Motor (63.8%) imagery were reported most frequently, while, Olfactory (4.9%) and Gustatory (2.2%) imagery occurred only rarely.
Participants also associated their imagery with a broad range of emotional experiences, with Happy (40.7%), Calm (31.1%), Energetic (30.7%) representing the most frequently reported emotions.

To characterise the diversity of imagery experiences elicited by each musical excerpt, Shannon entropy and the number of unique imagery patterns were calculated from the complete combinations of imagery elements, sensory modalities, and imagery-associated emotions selected by participants.
Lower entropy values indicate greater agreement among participants regarding the imagery content associated with a stimulus, whereas higher values reflect a wider diversity of imagery experiences.

Across the database, imagery elements exhibited a mean entropy of 2.74 (SD = 0.25; range = 2.11-3.23), sensory modalities showed a mean entropy of 2.76 (SD = 0.17; range = 2.36-3.10), and imageryassociated emotions yielded a mean entropy of 3.02 (SD = 0.18; range = 2.51-3.35).
The number of unique imagery patterns ranged from 11-27 for elements, 12-24 for sensory modalities and 14-29 for imagery-associated emotions across the stimuli.
These measures quantify the extent to which individual excerpts evoke stereotyped versus diverse imagery experiences.

Overall prevalence of the qualitative characteristics of MEMI: (A) imagery elements, (B) sensory modalities, and (C) imagery-associated emotions reported by participants across all trials in which mental imagery was experienced
Finally, we characterised the phenomenological content of MEMI by exploring the participant openended descriptions of imagery they experienced while listening to each musical excerpt.

These descriptions were analysed to quantify the level of detail in participants' accounts using word count, the extent to which they used concrete versus abstract language using lexical concreteness (Brysbaert et al., 2014), and the degree of lexical-semantic convergence across participants' descriptions of the same musical excerpts using TF-IDF-weighted lexical representations and pairwise cosine similarity.
text.formatted: These descriptions were analysed to quantify the level of detail in participants' accounts using word count, the extent to which they used concrete versus abstract language using lexical concreteness <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Brysbaert et al., 2014)</ref>, and the degree of lexical-semantic convergence across participants' descriptions of the same musical excerpts using TF-IDF-weighted lexical representations and pairwise cosine similarity.

text.text: 1501 imagery descriptions were analysed.

Descriptions contained a mean of 32.19 words (SD = 23.39; Mdn = 26; range = 1-201 words), suggesting considerable variability in the level of details participants used when describing their mental imagery.

Lexical concreteness of imagery descriptions yielded a mean score of 2.59 (SD = 0.29; range = 1.28-4.31) suggesting that imagery descriptions varied in the concreteness of vocabulary used to communicate participants' experiences across perceptual content or abstract experiential.

Few representative examples of the text reports of the participants' imagery experiences, based on their ratings of vividness, narrativity, movement and emotion intensity variables are provided in Table 2.

text.text: Of the 1501 imagery descriptions, 1395 met the criteria for the lexical-semantic similarity analysis.
Mean within-stimulus cosine similarity across the 60 excerpts was 0.0217 (SD = 0.0087, range = 0.0098-0.0570).
Absolute lexical overlap was generally low, with a median pairwise similarity of 0, indicating that most individual descriptions shared little direct lexical content.
Nevertheless, withinstimulus convergence was greater than expected under random assignment of stimulus identities.

To characterise the acoustic properties of the stimulus set, 54 acoustic descriptors spanning dynamics, fluctuation, rhythm, spectral, cepstral, timbre, and tonal domains were analysed.
Pairwise Pearson correlations indicated that the selected feature set exhibited relatively low redundancy, with only three descriptor pairs showing correlations exceeding |r| = .90.
PCA was therefore performed to identify the major latent dimensions underlying the acoustic variability across the musical excerpts.
Horn's parallel analysis indicated that six principal components should be retained, explaining 57.5% of the total variance in the acoustic feature space.

Following oblimin rotation, the components were interpreted as representing Spectral Brightness (21.47%), Dynamic Energy (10.37%), Tonal Structure (7.58%), Rhythmic Organization (7.05%), Acoustic Texture (5.99%), and Cepstral Characteristics (5.07%), based on their highest loading descriptors (see MUSIMAGINE repository: https://osf.io/z2kry/overview?view_only=bcd3ff22b3624132b2e3bddd22e85548).

text.text: Together, these six components provided a compact and interpretable representation of the acoustic diversity of the stimulus set.
The validated dataset developed in the present study has been organised into an openly accessible database named MUSIMAGINE, designed to facilitate future research on MEMI.

The complete database, accompanying documentation, and analysis resources are freely available through the Open Science Framework (MUSIMAGINE repository: https://osf.io/z2kry/overview?view_only=bcd3ff22b3624132b2e3bddd22e85548).
text.formatted: The complete database, accompanying documentation, and analysis resources are freely available through the Open Science Framework (MUSIMAGINE repository: <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/z2kry/overview?view_only=bcd3ff22b3624132b2e3bddd22e85548">https://osf.io/z2kry/</ref>).

text.text: We intend MUSIMAGINE to be a continuously expanding database with new music diversity, additional annotations and enhanced functionalities.
MUSIMAGINE is characterised by the following main features: 1) The database consists of 60 music excerpts across valence-arousal quadrant.

Stimulus validations measures accompany each excerpt, included the intended emotional classification, agreement statistics, and imagery occurrence rates, enabling researchers to select musical excerpts according to the reliability with which they evoke the desired emotional and imagery characteristics 2) Behavioural ratings including average ratings of perceived valence, arousal, liking, familiarity, and the six phenomenological dimensions of MEMI (ease, vividness, clarity, narrativity, movement, and emotion intensity).

3) Qualitative imagery annotations are available for each excerpt, including the frequency of each reported imagery elements, sensory modalities, imagery-associated emotions and raw data of anonymised open-ended descriptions of participants' imagery experiences.
These data provide opportunities to investigate both structure and naturalistic aspects of MEMI.

4) Acoustic annotations are provided for each musical excerpt, including the extracted 54 acoustic features and the 6 principal component scores describing broad acoustic characteristics of the music.
These measures support investigations linking musical structure to imagery experiences.

5) Participant-level information includes measure of sensory imagery ability (PSIQ), music background like training, music reward, and music associations, along with demographics like age, gender, native country, language etc, allowing researchers to examine how individual differences contribute to MEMI.
6) Open-access datasets and analysis resources include raw data, participant-level data, stimuluslevel summaries, acoustic annotations, questionnaires, codebooks, and analysis.
The final objective was to identify the factors associated with the occurrence of MEMI and inspect the capacity of the database to ask further research questions.

To address this, we examined whether imagery occurrence was predicted by 1) participants' subjective evaluations of the musical excerpts, 2) individual differences in imagery ability and musical background, and 3) acoustic features of music using generalised linear mixed-effects models with participants and stimulus as random intercepts.
The model including standardised values of perceived valence, arousal, liking and familiarity provided a significantly better fit than the null model (χ²(4) = 273.14, p < .001; marginal R² = .291).
text.formatted: The model including standardised values of perceived valence, arousal, liking and familiarity provided a significantly better fit than the null model (χ²(4) = 273.14, p < .001; marginal R² = .291).

text.text: Higher perceived valence (β = 0.28, SE = 0.13, χ²(1) = 4.41, p = .036), arousal (β = 0.23, SE = 0.10, χ²(1) = 5.21, p = .022), liking (β = 0.31, SE = 0.14, χ²(1) = 4.69, p = .030) and familiarity (β = 1.08, SE = 0.12, χ²(1) = 76.93, p < .001) were each associated with an increased likelihood of reporting MEMI, with familiarity emerging as the strongest predictor.
text.formatted: Higher perceived valence (β = 0.28, SE = 0.13, χ²(1) = 4.41, p = .036), arousal (β = 0.23, SE = 0.10, χ²(1) = 5.21, p = .022), liking (β = 0.31, SE = 0.14, χ²(1) = 4.69, p = .030) and familiarity (β = 1.08, SE = 0.12, χ²(1) = 76.93, p < .001) were each associated with an increased likelihood of reporting MEMI, with familiarity emerging as the strongest predictor.

text.text: Participant characteristics also significantly improved prediction of imagery occurrence relative to the null model (χ²(8) = 22.67, p = .004; marginal R² = .068).
The model included sensory imagery ability (PSIQ), years of musical training, and six questionnaire items assessing the music background, reward and associations with music.
Greater imagery ability, as measured by PSIQ, was associated with an increased likelihood of reporting MEMI (β = 0.27, SE = 0.13, χ²(1) = 4.53, p = .033).

Additionally, stronger agreement with the statement "I get emotional listening to certain pieces of music" was positively associated with imagery occurrence (β = 0.49, SE = 0.18, χ²(1) = 7.12, p = .008).
Years of musical training and the remaining music background items were not significant predictors.
The final model examined whether the acoustic properties of the musical excerpts predicted imagery occurrence.
The six principal components derived from the acoustic feature analysis were used as fixed effects in a generalised linear mixed-effects model.
The inclusion of the acoustic components did not significantly improve model fit relative to the null model (χ²(6) = 0.91, p = .989; marginal R² = .001).

None of the six acoustic principal components significantly predicted imagery occurrence (all p-values > .60), indicating that the broad acoustic dimensions identified within the stimulus set were not associated with whether listeners reported experiencing MEMI.
text.formatted: None of the six acoustic principal components significantly predicted imagery occurrence (all p-values > .60), indicating that the broad acoustic dimensions identified within the stimulus set were not associated with whether listeners reported experiencing MEMI.

text.text: These findings suggest that the occurrence of MEMI was primarily associated with listeners' subjective evaluations of the music and individual imagery ability, whereas the music background and associations as well as broad acoustic dimensions of musical excerpts did not contribute significantly to predicting imagery occurrence.
The present study introduces MUSIMAGINE, an open-access database of musical excerpts developed to support systematic investigation of Music-evoked Mental Imagery (MEMI).

By combining multidimensional imagery measures, qualitative descriptions, subjective evaluations of music appraisals, participant characteristics, and acoustic annotations, MUSIMAGINE provides a resource for investigating MEMI from behavioural, phenomenological, and computational perspectives.
The findings demonstrate that imagery was frequently reported in response to the selected excerpts, although its phenomenological characteristics and reported content varied across experiences.

Imagery occurrence was also associated with listeners' subjective evaluation of music and individual differences in sensory imagery ability, whereas the broad acoustic components examined did not significantly predict imagery occurrence.
Together, these findings highlight the multifaceted nature of MEMI and demonstrate the value of characterising imagery alongside listeners' subjective experiences and individual differences.

By making the database and its accompanying annotations openly accessible, the present study provides a foundation for reproducible research, systematic comparisons across studies, and further investigation of the factors associated with the phenomena.
A major methodological contribution of the present study is the development of a standardised resource specifically designed for studying MEMI.

Although previous studies have demonstrated that music can evoke imagery, many have relied on bespoke or ad hoc stimulus sets assembled to address individual research questions, making direct comparisons across studies and the accumulation of comparable evidence challenging (Belfi, 2019; Herff et al., 2021; Margulis et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Although previous studies have demonstrated that music can evoke imagery, many have relied on bespoke or ad hoc stimulus sets assembled to address individual research questions, making direct comparisons across studies and the accumulation of comparable evidence challenging <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Belfi, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Herff et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Margulis et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The present study addresses this limitation by providing a curated set of musical stimuli accompanied by multidimensional annotations, a common experimental protocol, and openly accessible data and analysis resources.
The scientific value of such a resource extends beyond the availability of musical excerpts to the quality and scope of their accompanying annotations.

Therefore, in the present study, we evaluated the intended emotional categorisations of the musical excerpts by comparing the researcher-assigned categories with listeners' perceived valence and arousal ratings.
The ratings broadly differentiated the intended emotional categories, although some excerpts deviated from their originally assigned quadrants.

The original labels are retained alongside the reassigned labels based on participant ratings and the numerical mean valence and arousal ratings by the participants, allowing researchers to select and analyse stimuli according to their specific questions.

For investigations of predictors of imagery and its associated dimensions, continuous ratings may be particularly informative because they preserve variation between the excerpts that would otherwise be obscured by categorical classification.
Second, imagery prevalence was high across the stimulus set, indicating that the selected excerpts frequently elicited the phenomenon they were selected to evoke.
Imagery occurrence varied across the individual excerpts but did not differ significantly across the emotional categories.

Together, these findings provide researchers with information about the emotional characteristics and imagery-evoking potential of individual excerpts, allowing them to be selected according to the specific requirements of future studies.
Beyond the characterisation of individual stimuli, MUSIMAGINE enables MEMI to be investigated within a unified framework across multiple complementary levels of analysis.

By integrating imagery occurrence, multidimensional phenomenological ratings, qualitative imagery descriptions, acoustic features, subjective music appraisals, and participant characteristics within a common experimental protocol, the MUSIMAGINE database facilitates investigations that extend beyond establishing whether imagery occurs.

Instead, it enables researchers to examine the nature of the imagery experienced, investigate musical and listener-related characteristics associated with these experiences, and explore relationships among these measures.
Beyond MEMI research, the availability of music stimuli characterised by listeners across various aspects may support broader research in the field of music perception and cognition.
In this way, MUSIMAGINE provides a shared empirical resource for investigating MEMI and potentially informing related areas of music research.
A central finding of the present study is that MEMI presence was a common response across the 60 musical excerpts examined.

Previous studies have documented a wide range of music-evoked imagery experiences, including visual scenes, auditory imagery, motor imagery, autobiographical memories, narratives, and other internally generated representations (Beaty et al., 2013; Küssner & Eerola, 2019; Margulis et al., 2019; Nanay, 2022).
text.formatted: Previous studies have documented a wide range of music-evoked imagery experiences, including visual scenes, auditory imagery, motor imagery, autobiographical memories, narratives, and other internally generated representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Beaty et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Küssner & Eerola, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Margulis et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Nanay, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The present work extends this literature by characterising these diverse forms of imagery within a common set of musical excerpts and an integrated measurement framework.
The stimuli were selected to encompass music from different genres, moods, and emotion characteristics, rather than on the basis of established evidence that they would reliably evoke imagery.
The high prevalence of imagery reports therefore emerged from testing this varied stimulus set, rather than being an outcome built into the selection procedure.

Nevertheless, because the excerpts were not sampled to represent the full range of music that exists, the prevalence observed here should not be interpreted as an estimate of MEMI occurrence across music more generally.
Frequent reports of imagery did not imply uniform experiences.
Substantial variation was observed in the phenomenological characteristics of the experiences both between listeners and across musical excerpts.
Listeners differed in the ease with which imagery emerged, its vividness and clarity, the extent to which it unfolded as a narrative, the degree of perceived movement, and its emotion intensity.

Therefore, the empirical contribution of the study indicates that although the selected excerpts frequently elicited imagery, the experiences they evoked varied considerably in their subjective qualities.

From an experimental perspective, this balance between consistency and diversity represents a considerable strength, as it provides sufficient experimental control while preserving the natural variability required to examine mechanisms underlying imagery generation.
The relationship among the six imagery dimensions provides further insight into this variation.
Rather than capturing a single, uniform aspect of imagery, the dimensions were associated to different degrees.
Specifically, the strong associations among ease, vividness, clarity and narrativity suggest that these characteristics may share aspect of subjective imagery quality.

This observation is consistent with broader mental imagery research, where vividness and clarity have frequently been used as core indicators of imagery quality, and ease of imagery generation has similarly been linked to the strength of internally generated representations (Gelding et al., 2023; Herff et al., 2021).
text.formatted: This observation is consistent with broader mental imagery research, where vividness and clarity have frequently been used as core indicators of imagery quality, and ease of imagery generation has similarly been linked to the strength of internally generated representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Gelding et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Herff et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, movement and emotion intensity showed comparatively weaker associations with the other dimensions, suggesting that they capture additional aspects of the experience.

One plausible interpretation is that ease, vividness, clarity, and narrativity primarily describe the subjective quality and organisation of an imagined experience, whereas movement and emotion intensity capture its dynamic and affective characteristics.
The exploratory PCA provides evidence to support that, and a further investigation would be useful to establish a definitive structure of imagery dimensions.
The characterisation of MEMI across the multiple response measures further illustrates the diversity and complexity of the reported imagery experiences.

Across the selected imagery elements, sensory modalities, imagery-associated emotions, participants reported a rich variety of experiences characterised by people, places, movements, autobiographical memories, emotions, and multisensory representations.
These results suggest that music gives rise to integrated mental simulations in which perceptual, emotional, and mnemonic information is brought together into coherent experiences.

One possible explanation underlying this diversity is semantic priming, whereby musical cues may activate networks of semantically related concepts, memories, emotions and sensory representations that together contribute to the construction of imagined events (Groves et al., 2025; Margulis & Jakubowski, 2024).
text.formatted: One possible explanation underlying this diversity is semantic priming, whereby musical cues may activate networks of semantically related concepts, memories, emotions and sensory representations that together contribute to the construction of imagined events <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Groves et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Margulis & Jakubowski, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: These activated representations provide the building blocks from which more elaborate imagined experiences can be constructed.

Our interpretation aligns with the views from the previous literature arguing that music serves not merely as an auditory stimulus but as a powerful cue for activating interconnected knowledge structures and cognition (Jakubowski et al., 2024; Owen et al., 2024; Taruffi & Küssner, 2019).
text.formatted: Our interpretation aligns with the views from the previous literature arguing that music serves not merely as an auditory stimulus but as a powerful cue for activating interconnected knowledge structures and cognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Jakubowski et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Owen et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Taruffi & Küssner, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, this interpretation emerged consistently across both structured response measures and unrestricted descriptions, increasing confidence that the heterogenous nature of MEMI reflects a robust characteristic of the phenomenon rather than an artefact of any single measure approach.
The open-ended descriptions of MEMI extend beyond the activation of individual semantic concepts.

The coherent scenes, fictional narratives, emotionally meaningful events, and autobiographical experiences reported by the participants imply that these activated representations are organised into internally cohesive simulations.

This aligns closely with the constructive episodic simulation hypothesis, which proposes that episodic memory supports the flexible recombination of stored experiences into novel imagined events (Gaesser, 2013; Hashim et al., 2024; Schacter et al., 2007).
text.formatted: This aligns closely with the constructive episodic simulation hypothesis, which proposes that episodic memory supports the flexible recombination of stored experiences into novel imagined events <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Gaesser, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Hashim et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Schacter et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: From this perspective, music may not simply retrieve existing memories or concepts but provide a scaffold upon which new internally generated experiences are constructed.
Such a constructive account is also compatible with broader theories of internally directed cognition.

The default mode network (DMN), for example, has been implicated in mental re-constructions, future simulations and spontaneous mind wandering during music listening (Fox & Beaty, 2019; Kosslyn et al., 2001; Taruffi et al., 2017).
text.formatted: The default mode network (DMN), for example, has been implicated in mental re-constructions, future simulations and spontaneous mind wandering during music listening <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Fox & Beaty, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Kosslyn et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Taruffi et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these perspectives suggest that MEMI may emerge from distributed cognitive systems supporting internally generated thought rather than reflecting an isolated response to musical stimulation.
Although the present study was not designed to directly test these mechanisms, the present findings are broadly consistent with this interpretation.
This study, therefore, provides a behavioural and phenomenological basis for future investigations of the cognitive and neural processes underlying MEMI.
Having established that imagery was frequently reported in response to the selected musical excerpts, an important question concerns the factors associated with whether these experiences occur.

To address this, the present study examined three classes of predictors: listeners' subjective appraisal of the music (valence, arousal, liking, familiarity), individual differences in imagery ability and musicrelated characteristics, and the acoustic properties of the musical excerpts.
The findings suggest that the occurrence of MEMI cannot be understood solely as a property of the musical stimulus.

Alternatively, the occurrence of MEMI appears to emerge through an interaction between the characteristics of the music, the listener's subjective experiences of that music, and the individual differences in imagery ability.
These findings point towards a perspective in which MEMI reflects the relationship between musical stimuli, listeners' subjective experiences, and individual cognitive characteristics.
Among the examined predictors, listeners' subjective evaluations of the musical excerpts showed the strongest associations with imagery occurrence.
Music perceived as more familiar, better liked, more pleasant and more energetic was associated with a greater likelihood of reporting imagery.
This suggests that the subjective experience of music plays a central role in imagery generation.
Rather than being associated solely with the acoustic properties of the stimulus, imagery occurrence was also related to how listeners evaluated and experienced the music.

This interpretation is consistent with research on musical aesthetics, which emphasises that the aesthetic experiences involve listeners' appraisals and interpretations of musical characteristics alongside perceptual, emotional, cognitive and contextual information (Belfi, 2019; Cowen et al., 2020; Juslin, 2013).
text.formatted: This interpretation is consistent with research on musical aesthetics, which emphasises that the aesthetic experiences involve listeners' appraisals and interpretations of musical characteristics alongside perceptual, emotional, cognitive and contextual information <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Belfi, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Cowen et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Juslin, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Within this framework, the subjective evaluations may be viewed as complementary aspects of this appraisal process that in turn facilitate the transition from auditory perception to internally generated mental experiences.

Interestingly, whereas previous work has shown that the vividness of imagery contributes to aesthetic appreciation of music, the present findings suggest possibility of a reverse relationship that aesthetic appraisal may itself assist the emergence of mental imagery (Belfi, 2019; Taruffi, 2021).
text.formatted: Interestingly, whereas previous work has shown that the vividness of imagery contributes to aesthetic appreciation of music, the present findings suggest possibility of a reverse relationship that aesthetic appraisal may itself assist the emergence of mental imagery <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Belfi, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Taruffi, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: More importantly, familiarity emerged as the strongest predictor of imagery occurrence.

Familiar music may activate richer semantic associations, memories, emotions, and archetypes accumulated through previous exposures of music listening, media, language, and everyday life (Cowen et al., 2020; Curwen, 2025; Groves et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Familiar music may activate richer semantic associations, memories, emotions, and archetypes accumulated through previous exposures of music listening, media, language, and everyday life <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Cowen et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Curwen, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Groves et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In sum, these findings propose that subjective appraisal represents a critical intermediary between musical structure and MEMI.
Individual differences also contributed to the occurrence of MEMI.
Participants with greater sensory imagery ability were more likely to report experiencing mental imagery during music listening.
This finding suggests that individual differences in the capacity to generate mental imagery are relevant to whether imagery is reported in response to music (Curwen, 2025; Hashim et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This finding suggests that individual differences in the capacity to generate mental imagery are relevant to whether imagery is reported in response to music <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Curwen, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Hashim et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Surprisingly, neither formal musical expertise nor most aspects of musical background, reward and associations predicted imagery occurrence.
The exception was emotional responsiveness to music: participants who reported being more emotionally affected by music were more likely to report imagery.

This result complements the associations observed for subjective music appraisals and suggests that both imagery ability and emotional responsiveness may be relevant to individual differences in MEMI.
Thus, while the selected musical excerpts provided opportunities for imagery to occur, the likelihood of reporting imagery also varied with listeners' cognitive and emotional characteristics.
In contrast to previous studies, the broad latent acoustic dimensions described in the present study did not directly predict imagery occurrence.

While prior works have extensively reported associations between individual acoustic characteristics and MEMI (Ayyildiz, Milne, et al., 2025; Cowen et al., 2020; Dahl et al., 2023; Groves et al., 2025; Herff et al., 2021), this apparent discrepancy should be interpreted in light of the present study design.
text.formatted: While prior works have extensively reported associations between individual acoustic characteristics and MEMI <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Ayyildiz, Milne, et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Cowen et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Dahl et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Groves et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Herff et al., 2021)</ref>, this apparent discrepancy should be interpreted in light of the present study design.

text.text: The objective of the database was not to include all forms of music, but rather to establish a collection of musical excerpts capable of reliably eliciting MEMI.
Therefore, the selected stimuli already occupied a relatively restricted region of the broader acoustic space with respect to their imagery-evoking capacity.
Under these conditions, broad differences in acoustic structure may contribute less to explaining whether imagery occurs than they would in a more acoustically heterogeneous collection of music.
Instead, acoustic properties may play a more prominent role in shaping the characteristics of imagery, such as its vividness, emotion intensity or movement, which require separate investigation.
In summary, the findings suggest that imagery occurrence cannot be attributed to any single determinant.

While broad acoustic dimensions did not directly predict imagery occurrence, preliminary results suggested that there were several associations between the broad acoustic dimensions and the subjective appraisal ratings.
While these results were beyond the scope of this study, nevertheless, it suggests the contribution of acoustic features in shaping how music is emotionally and aesthetically experienced.
In turn, these appraisals, together with the listener's cognitive capacity for imagery, appear to influence whether music develops into a rich internally generated experience.

This interactional perspective highlights MEMI not as a simple consequence of either the music or the listener alone, but as an emergent phenomenon arising from the reciprocal relationship between musical structure, psychological experience, and individual cognitive characteristics.
The main objective of this paper was to provide a systematic structure for investigating MEMI through a curated and validated database of musical stimuli.

By integrating standardised behavioural measures, qualitative descriptions, subjective evaluation, participant characteristics and acoustic annotations within a single experimental protocol, we provide a methodological foundation upon which future MEMI research can be built.
The MUSIMAGINE database enables researchers to investigate complementary levels of the phenomenon either independently or in combination.
This flexibility allows studies to address diverse theoretical questions while maintaining methodological consistency, thereby improving the comparability and cumulative development of MEMI research.

By making both the database and the accompanying analysis resources openly available, the present work also contributes to broader efforts promoting transparency, reproducibility, and open science within music cognition research.
The present work also advances the empirical understanding of MEMI itself.
Beyond demonstrating that music is capable of evoking mental imagery, we characterise MEMI as a common, multidimensional, and phenomenologically rich consequence of music listening.

By integrating quantitative and qualitative measures within a single skeleton, the study demonstrates that imagery should not be described by its occurrence alone but should instead be understood through the interaction of its perceptual, emotional and semantic characteristics.

This broader empirical characterisation provides a more comprehensive basis for future studies seeking to explain not whether music evokes imagery, but also the nature and diversity of the experiences that it evokes.
Perhaps the key contribution of the present work is the conceptual understanding of the framework explaining the emergence of MEMI.

Collectively, the findings support that MEMI is best understood as an emergent phenomenon arising through interactions between musical structure, the listener's subjective appraisal of the music, and individual cognitive characteristics.

This perspective shifts the arguments from viewing imagery as a direct consequence of either the musical stimulus or the listener to understanding MEMI as the product of multiple interacting processes.

Although the present framework requires further empirical evaluation, it provides a coherent theoretical cornerstone for integrating future behavioural, phenomenological, computational, and neuroscientific investigations of MEMI within a common conceptual perspective.
The MUSIMAGINE database represents a crucial first step towards the systematic investigation of MEMI; however, several considerations should guide its continued development.
Foremost, the resource was intentionally constructed from musical excerpts expected to evoke MEMI rather than to represent the full diversity of musical experiences.
This design was necessary to establish a robust experimental foundation for investigating imagery but limits the current database to questions concerning imagery-evoking music.

Future iterations could incorporate comparison stimuli with lower imagery-evoking potential presumably with constant acoustic properties like monotones, vocal music, and a broader range of musical genres and traditions.

Such extensions would enable researchers to analyse how musical properties distinguish imagery-evoking from one-imagery-evoking music, while improving the ecological validity and generalisability of the resource.
A second priority concerns the continued expansion of the normative dataset.
The present database was validated using an adult participant sample and provides a foundation for characterising MEMI within this population.

Even though no restrictions were implied based on different developmental stages, ethnicity, sensory imagery ability, musical expertise, or clinical populations, the results within such contexts could provide thought-provoking insights.
Considering the standardised methodological structure of the database, additional datasets can be readily incorporated while preserving the comparability across studies and populations.
Importantly, MUSIMAGINE database should be entreated as evolving scientific resource rather than a static repository of musical excerpts.

Future developments could incorporate additional musical stimuli, richer acoustic and computational annotations, more detailed descriptions of imagery content, and supportive behavioural and neuroscientific measures.

The integration of physiological recordings, neuroimaging paradigms, and longitudinal or repeated-measures designs would further strengthen the resource by linking subjective imagery experiences to their underlying cognitive and neural mechanisms.

By maintaining an open-access framework, the present database is intended to evolve alongside theoretical and methodological advances in the field, providing an increasingly comprehensive foundation for future investigations of music-evoked mental imagery.

MUSIMAGINE provides an open-access resource for the systematic investigation of Music-Evoked Mental Imagery (MEMI), combining musical stimuli with multidimensional phenomenological measures, qualitative descriptions, listener appraisals, participant characteristics, and acoustic annotations.
The findings demonstrate that imagery was frequently reported in response to the selected excerpts, while the occurrence and phenomenological characteristics varied across stimuli.
Imagery occurrence was associated with listeners' subjective evaluations of music and individual differences in sensory imagery ability.

Although the acoustic features examined did not significantly predict imagery occurrence, the accompanying annotations offer opportunities to investigate the relationships between musical characteristics, listener characteristics, and imagery experiences in greater depth.
By making these data available within a common framework, MUSIMAGINE supports reproducible research and facilitates comparisons across studies.
